title: Wrapped
hook: A year of listening, handed back as a gift.
before: December was Spotify’s toughest month. People broke their routines over the holidays and opened the app less, just when the company wanted new subscribers.
idea: In December 2016 Spotify sent each listener a recap of their year: the artists they loved, how much they listened, and a ‘Your Top Songs of 2016’ playlist. A simpler ‘Year in Music’ had run in 2015.
shift: Listening data became something people wanted to show off. Wrapped has returned every December since, and it has grown from a campaign into a cultural event of its own.
measure: New Premium subscribers credited to the 2016 campaign in Spotify’s Cannes effectiveness entry
evidence: Spotify reports 5.9m new Premium subscribers, conversions up 50% on the year before and faster growth in monthly users, reversing the usual December dip. These are the company’s own figures in an awards entry, and the summary doesn’t separate Wrapped from Spotify’s other December activity.
lesson: If your product already holds a story about each customer, hand it back to them and they will do the distribution.
test: The entry compares December 2016 with earlier Decembers on subscriptions, conversions and monthly users. It is a before-and-after comparison, not a controlled test.
memorable: It flatters the listener. The data says something about you, and sharing it says something about you too.

creative.label: Watch Spotify’s 2016 Wrapped film at The One Show
creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the Cannes effectiveness summary · WARC
take: Wrapped is the best data campaign of its era and a reminder of how much a company knows about you. Both are true, and the second is why it has to stay this generous.

image.credit: Spotify, 2016 Wrapped recap email · still from The One Show entry

title: The Pepsi Challenge
hook: A sip test that turned taste into a statistic.
before: Pepsi was fighting Coca-Cola, the bigger and older brand, in what became known as the cola wars.
idea: From 1975 Pepsi set up blind taste tests in public. Shoppers sipped two unmarked colas, picked a favourite and were then shown which one they had chosen.
shift: The argument moved from image to evidence. If people preferred Pepsi with the labels off, the label was all Coke had left.
measure: The challenge has run, on and off, since 1975. A milestone, not a result
evidence: Pepsi’s claims rest on its own tests, run single-blind, so the people serving the colas knew which was which. Later research found that tasters tend to prefer the sweeter drink after a single sip, which suits Pepsi. No reliable public figure isolates the challenge’s effect on sales.
lesson: A claim built on data is only as strong as the method behind it, and rivals will check the method.
test: There is no published effectiveness paper. The record is the taste test itself and the arguments about how it was run.
links: Watch an earlier US Pepsi Challenge advert (1978 archive upload)
memorable: It turns the viewer into the judge. You can’t watch it without wondering which cup you would pick.

creative.label: Watch Challenge John (UK, 1983) at the History of Advertising Trust

take: The cleverest claim in this edition, and the shakiest proof. Coca-Cola’s eventual answer, New Coke, belongs in Edition 05.

image.alt: Two unmarked cola cups on a Pepsi Challenge table with a crowd behind it
image.credit: Pepsi, Challenge John (UK, 1983) · History of Advertising Trust

title: Lasts Longer
hook: A battery that sold a measurement.
before: In 1978 Duracell had about 4% of the UK battery market. Few people knew the brand, and fewer cared about battery quality.
idea: The advertising compared Duracell with ordinary zinc-carbon batteries and showed the performance gap on screen.
shift: A dull purchase became a contest you could watch. By 1989 Duracell led the market with more than 30%, and it held a price premium.
measure: Share of the UK battery market by 1989, up from 4% in 1978, per the 1990 IPA paper
evidence: Penetration rose from 24% in 1980 to 61% in 1989, and share from 4% to more than 30%, with a price premium held throughout. The paper reports trends and awareness rather than a modelled estimate of the advertising’s own effect.
lesson: If your product wins a test, make the test the advertising.
test: The 1990 paper tracks penetration, share, awareness and price across a decade, and uses 1989 research to show the campaign hadn’t worn out.
links: Watch a later UK race ad on Duracell’s channel
memorable: It turns an invisible quality, how long a battery lasts, into something you watch happen.

creative.label: Watch the 1979 drumming-bunnies advert on YouTube

take: Long before anyone said ‘data-driven’, Duracell built a decade of advertising on one test result.

image.alt: Rows of pink Duracell bunnies playing drums
image.credit: Duracell drumming-bunnies commercial (1979) · Bionic Disco archive upload

title: The Advantage Card
hook: A late loyalty card that paid its way quickly.
before: Boots came to loyalty cards later than other retailers.
idea: The Advantage Card rewarded shoppers with points and gave Boots a record of what each member bought. J. Walter Thompson’s advertising built awareness of the card fast.
shift: The card became part of how Boots worked. By March 1998 Boots credited 8% of its sales to it, and it was shaping the company’s strategy.
measure: Share of Boots sales credited to the Advantage Card by March 1998, per the IPA paper
evidence: Boots credited 8% of its sales to the card within months, and the paper links it to 19% growth in shareholder value. Sales made with a card are not the same as extra sales, and the summary doesn’t estimate how many would have happened anyway.
lesson: A loyalty scheme is a data product first. The advertising’s job is to make people want to carry it.
test: The paper tracks card awareness and the share of sales made with the card, and argues the scheme might not have survived without the advertising.
memorable: It made a data relationship feel like a reward. Members saw points, and Boots saw what they bought.
metric_label: Share of sales made with the card
take: The card did the persuading here. The advertising only had to get it into people’s purses and wallets.
credit: IPA 1998 · 1 Star · J. Walter Thompson for Boots The Chemist

image.alt: Blue and multicoloured launch artwork showing Boots Advantage Cards and shopping illustrations
image.credit: Boots Advantage Card launch artwork (1997) · Boots Heritage

title: The UltraLift Challenge
hook: A face cream that handed customers the ruler.
before: UltraLift had lost 30% of its sales in four years. Garnier had scientific proof that it worked, but shoppers had stopped believing the science in anti-ageing ads.
idea: Publicis skipped the ‘labcoat lecture’ and challenged women to try the cream for 14 days. Each sample kit came with a ‘Wrinkle Reader’, so people could measure their own skin before and after.
shift: The proof moved from the lab to the bathroom mirror, and real people talked about their own results.
measure: Revenue return on marketing investment reported in the IPA case
evidence: Unit sales rose 40% within 18 months, penetration rose 16%, and 239,000 people asked for a sample kit. The £1.91 is revenue rather than profit, and the summary doesn’t describe how it was modelled.
lesson: When people stop trusting your data, let them make their own.
test: The case tracks sample-kit requests, unit sales and penetration from the start of the challenge and reports a revenue return on the marketing.
memorable: The Wrinkle Reader makes the customer the scientist.

creative.label: Watch the 2012 UltraLift Challenge advert with Davina McCall on YouTube

take: This is the one I’d steal. If your audience is sick of your statistics, give them the means to produce their own.
credit: IPA 2014 · Bronze · Publicis London for L’Oréal

image.alt: Garnier UltraLift Challenge sign and campaign web address above a crowd
image.credit: Garnier and Publicis, UltraLift Challenge with Davina McCall (2012) · archive upload

title: Recipe Receipt
hook: A till receipt that told you what to cook.
before: Most Brazilian households had a jar of Hellmann’s in the fridge, but they didn’t buy it often. The brand needed people to use more of it.
idea: Ogilvy Brazil linked a recipe database to supermarket tills. When a shopper bought Hellmann’s, the receipt printed a recipe using it and other items in their basket.
shift: The receipt, the most ignored piece of paper in a shop, became a prompt to use the product.
measure: Sales increase in the selected stores, per the APG case on WARC
evidence: Sales rose 44% in the stores taking part, according to the case. Results from a small number of selected stores are an early sign rather than proof of a wider effect, and the summary doesn’t say what they were compared with.
lesson: The best place for an idea is the moment the customer is already holding in their hand.
test: The case reports sales in the selected stores during the activity. It is a store-level trial, not a controlled national test.
memorable: It uses data people never think of as data: their own shopping list.

creative.label: Watch ‘Recipe Receipt’ on Ogilvy Brazil’s channel
creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the APG case summary · WARC
take: A tiny idea with a big lesson. The data you already have is often more useful than the data you wish you had.
data_source: What was in the shopping basket

image.alt: An itemised supermarket receipt with Hellmann’s mayonnaise circled
image.credit: Hellmann’s and Ogilvy Brazil, Recipe Receipt (2012) · still from the D&AD archive

title: Live Appeals
hook: Urgent appeals, shown in the region where someone went missing.
before: Around 250,000 people go missing in the UK each year. Missing People had a small budget, so its appeals reached few people.
idea: In 2012 the charity and the Outdoor Media Centre began putting urgent appeals on digital outdoor screens donated by media owners, regionalised so each appeal appeared where it mattered.
shift: A charity with almost no media money gained a national network of screens that could publish an appeal instantly.
measure: Increase in the number of people found safe and well, per the IPA case
evidence: The case reports 22% more people found safe and well, 226% more contacts with the charity and 38% higher awareness. Many things affect whether someone is found, and the summary doesn’t isolate the screens’ contribution.
lesson: Data about place and time can matter more than a big budget.
test: The case compares outcomes before and after the partnership began. It is a trend, not a controlled comparison.
memorable: It treats outdoor media like a newsroom, publishing the moment the story breaks.

creative.label: Watch Missing People Weekly Appeals at Grand Visual
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: More people found safe and well
take: The most important number in this edition isn’t a return on investment. It’s people found.
credit: IPA case, 2014 · Missing People and the Outdoor Media Centre
data_source: Where and when someone went missing

image.alt: Kate McCann standing near a digital Missing People billboard at the launch
image.credit: Missing People and the Outdoor Media Centre, 2012 launch photograph · Grand Visual

title: Look Up
hook: A billboard that knew which plane was overhead.
before: Flying had become routine. ‘Look Up’ was part of British Airways’ wider ‘Magic of Flying’ campaign, which set out to bring back some of the wonder.
idea: OgilvyOne London built digital billboards in Piccadilly Circus and Chiswick that tracked BA flights. When one passed overhead, a child on screen got up and pointed at it, with its flight number and where it had come from.
shift: An ad that would normally ask you to look at it asked you to look at the sky.
measure: The campaign ran on two sites. A scale fact, not a result
evidence: The public record is about fame: awards including a D&AD Yellow Pencil, and widely shared films. No published figure links the billboards to bookings or brand measures.
lesson: Real-time data is most powerful when it shows people something true about the world around them.
test: There is no effectiveness paper in the public record. Its success is measured in coverage and awards.
memorable: The child’s gesture does the work. Everyone has pointed at a plane, and everyone looks up when someone else does.

creative.label: Watch ‘#lookup in Piccadilly Circus’ on British Airways’ channel

metric_label: Billboards, at Piccadilly Circus and Chiswick
take: Probably the most beautiful use of data here, and the least proven. Both of those are worth knowing.
credit: D&AD 2014 · Yellow Pencil · OgilvyOne Worldwide London for British Airways

image.alt: The child on the British Airways billboard at Piccadilly Circus pointing towards a plane
image.credit: British Airways and OgilvyOne, Look Up (2013) · still from British Airways’ film

title: Swap & Save Challenge
hook: A supermarket that let shoppers’ savings make the argument.
before: Aldi’s ‘Like Brands’ campaign had improved views of its quality. By 2013 range perception and social stigma were still holding shoppers back.
idea: The Swap & Save Challenge followed real shoppers as they moved their main shop to Aldi and showed how much they saved.
shift: Shopping at Aldi stopped looking like a compromise and started looking like common sense.
measure: Return on marketing investment in the UK, with £68m of incremental revenue, per the IPA case
evidence: Swap & Save contributed just under 15% of UK sales, £68m of incremental revenue and a ROMI of 4.72. In Ireland it contributed 8%, €11m and a ROMI of 8. The summary doesn’t say whether the returns are revenue or profit.
lesson: Let customers run the test, then measure what it did.
test: Econometrics estimated the campaign’s contribution to sales in each country and converted it into incremental revenue and a return.
memorable: Real people adding up their own savings carry more weight than any price claim a supermarket could make.

creative.label: Watch The Blakes, a later Irish Swap & Save advert, on Vimeo
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: Put this next to the Pepsi Challenge. Same idea, a customer test as the claim, but thirty-eight years later it comes with a model and a return.
credit: IPA 2014 · Silver · McCann Manchester for Aldi UK & Ireland

image.alt: Aldi Swap & Save artwork introducing the shoppers taking part in the challenge
image.credit: Aldi Swap & Save shopper artwork (2013) · reproduced by Gm&Co

title: Raising Eyebrows
hook: Ads written like headlines, placed next to the news that provoked them.
before: The Economist wanted younger readers. Its journalism was not in question. Getting new people to notice it was.
idea: Proximity London set up ‘newsrooms’ to write topical ad copy, and UM London used programmatic platforms to place it next to related news, reaching people when they were likely to be receptive.
shift: The advertising started to behave like the product: quick, topical and provocative.
measure: Paid subscriptions credited to the activity, worth £25 of revenue per £1 on projected lifetime value
evidence: The case credits the activity with 64,000 paid subscriptions and more than five million new retargetable users. The £25 return is revenue projected over subscribers’ lifetimes, so it depends on assumptions about how long they stay.
lesson: If your product is timely, let the advertising be timely too, and let data decide where it appears.
test: The case counts subscriptions attributed to the programmatic activity and values them using projected subscriber lifetime revenue.
memorable: Each ad reads like the start of an argument. It invites you to disagree, then to subscribe.

creative.label: Watch Raising Eyebrows and Subscriptions on Proximity London’s Vimeo channel
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: This is the case I’d show anyone who thinks brand and performance are separate jobs.
credit: IPA 2016 · Gold · Proximity London and UM for The Economist

image.alt: A red Economist digital ad about women becoming CEOs above a Guardian article
image.credit: The Economist and Proximity London, Raising Eyebrows digital ad · Direct New Ideas

title: Two Hot Days
hook: A pool builder that only advertised after two hot days in a row.
before: Pool sales in Australia were in long-term decline as homes became less affordable and more people lived in apartments.
idea: AFFINITY mined the data and found purchase enquiries rose after two or more days of higher-than-average temperatures. A weather feed switched the media on when those conditions arrived and off when they didn’t.
shift: The budget moved from the calendar to the weather, spending only when people were already thinking about a pool.
measure: Incremental ROI reported in the IPA case, with media spend cut by 30%
evidence: Leads rose 11% and sales 23% while media spend fell by 30%, for an incremental return of 54 to 1. The IPA summary describes it as a revenue return. A hot summer helps a pool business anyway, which is exactly what the estimate has to separate out.
lesson: Find the signal that comes before the sale, and spend only when it fires.
test: Media switched on and off with the weather, and results were compared with the year before.
memorable: It is the simplest data idea here. Nobody wants a pool on a cold day.

creative.label: Watch Diving into Data on AFFINITY’s Vimeo channel
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: A small business, a smaller budget and one of the best returns in the whole archive. Data isn’t only for big brands.
credit: IPA 2016 · Gold · AFFINITY for Narellan Pools

image.alt: Turquoise Diving into Data case film artwork with a diving mask
image.credit: Narellan Pools, Diving into Data · AFFINITY’s case film artwork

title: The Cough Predictor
hook: A cough remedy that advertised just before the coughs arrived.
before: New guidance said children shouldn’t be given cough and cold medicines, natural rivals multiplied, and mums tended to ‘wait and see’ before treating a cough.
idea: Search and social data revealed mothers’ doubt about coughs, which became the message, ‘Don’t ignore a cough’. AFFINITY then built an algorithm that predicted outbreaks of colds and switched programmatic ads on when coughs were likely to rise.
shift: The brand turned up at the moment the problem appeared, with a message aimed at the hesitation.
measure: Digital click-through compared with a control group, per the IPA case
evidence: Clicks ran 54% higher than a control group, and sales grew 10% in six months while the category fell 8.5% in a very warm winter. Market share rose 18.5%. The control group tests the targeting, and the sales figures are a trend set against the category.
lesson: Predict the need, then be the first brand there.
test: Ads served by the predictor were compared with a control group on click-through, and sales were tracked against a declining category.
links: Read the Australian Effie summary · WARC
memorable: The idea is all in the timing. The same ad a week later would have been too late.

creative.label: Watch Don’t Ignore a Cough on AFFINITY’s Vimeo channel
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: A control group in a cough remedy campaign. More brands should be this curious about whether their targeting works.

image.alt: Prospan print advert showing a child coughing in a room with a gathered crowd
image.credit: Flordis and AFFINITY, Don’t Ignore a Cough (2016) · reproduced by B&T

title: Hungerithm
medium: Pricing at 7-Eleven, social, TV and PR
hook: The angrier the internet, the cheaper the Snickers.
before: Chocolate bars had been declining in Australia for years, and millennials were drifting to bite-size and healthier snacks, or to whatever was on promotion.
idea: Clemenger BBDO Melbourne built the Hungerithm. It monitored the mood on Twitter and lowered the price of Snickers at 7-Eleven stores as people got angrier, a live version of ‘You’re not you when you’re hungry’.
shift: A price promotion became a piece of entertainment people checked and shared.
measure: Growth in Snickers sales at a key retailer, per the Australian Effie case
evidence: The case reports a reach of over 4 million 18 to 35 year olds and 10% sales growth at a key retailer. Other entries quote much bigger unit figures for 7-Eleven, so the measures differ by source. Either way it is a sales trend during a price promotion.
lesson: Put a familiar mechanic, a discount, inside an idea people want to watch.
test: The case reports Snickers sales at the retailer during the activity. A price cut lifts sales by itself, and the summary doesn’t separate that out.
memorable: It makes the internet’s bad mood useful. Every angry headline was a coupon.
impact_source: Read the Australian Effie summary · WARC
take: Brilliant fun, but it’s a discount with a story attached. I’d want to know how much the story added beyond the price cut.
credit: Australian Effie Awards 2017 · Bronze · Clemenger BBDO Melbourne for Mars Australia

image.alt: Three mobile screens with different Hungerithm prices and Snickers offer barcodes
image.credit: Snickers and Clemenger BBDO Melbourne, Hungerithm (2016) · still from The One Show entry

title: Whopper Detour
hook: A one-cent Whopper, unlocked only at McDonald’s.
before: Burger King had far fewer restaurants than McDonald’s and wanted more people to order through its app.
idea: FCB New York geofenced around 14,000 McDonald’s restaurants. Anyone who opened the Burger King app near one could order a Whopper for one cent, then collect it from the nearest Burger King.
shift: Its rival’s biggest strength, being everywhere, became the delivery mechanism for Burger King’s app.
measure: App downloads reported by Burger King’s parent company
evidence: Burger King’s parent company reported 1.5 million downloads, and the work won the Grand Effie in the US in 2020. The Effie entry also claims incremental revenue, which this archive couldn’t check against the original. Downloads show behaviour, not lasting sales.
lesson: Use your competitor’s scale as your media plan.
test: The public record counts downloads during the offer. A one-cent price explains much of the spike, which is why later sales matter more.
memorable: It’s a dare. To get the deal you had to stand outside McDonald’s and order a Burger King.

creative.label: Watch The Whopper Detour at The One Show

impact_source: See the Grand Effie announcement · Effie
take: The cheekiest idea in the edition. I’d still want to know how many of those downloads were ordering again a month later.
credit: Effie US 2020 · Grand Effie · FCB New York for Burger King

image.alt: An orange Detour Ahead sign with instructions to download the Burger King app
image.credit: Burger King, FCB New York and O Positive, The Whopper Detour (2018) · The One Show archive

title: Clubcard Prices
medium: TV, press, digital and in store
hook: A loyalty card that started lowering prices at the till.
before: Tesco had run Clubcard since 1995, and it had settled into being an established points scheme.
idea: In 2020 Tesco turned Clubcard into instant lower prices for members. BBH’s advertising showed shoppers with ‘the power to lower prices’ and their delighted ‘thrill face’, and data-driven media reached people who didn’t yet use the card, including by location.
shift: The card stopped being something you saved up for later and became a reason to choose Tesco today.
measure: Profit ROMI estimated for 2020 to 2023, alongside 10.7m new members, per the IPA case
evidence: The case estimates 10.7m new Clubcard members, a £627m net sales inflow and £3.38 of profit for every £1 invested between 2020 and 2023. Much of the value sits in the prices themselves, so the estimate has to separate the advertising from the offer.
lesson: If a loyalty scheme feels slow, make the reward immediate and make the advertising about the feeling.
test: The paper estimates new members, sales inflow and profit return for 2020 to 2023, including targeted media aimed at people who didn’t yet use the card.
memorable: The ‘thrill face’ turns a discount into a feeling you can see.

creative.label: Watch Feel the Power to Lower Prices on Sidekick’s Vimeo channel

take: Twenty-five years after it launched, Clubcard is still Tesco’s best data asset. This is when it started paying customers back on the spot.
credit: IPA 2024 · BBH and EssenceMediacom for Tesco

image.alt: A shopper strikes a superhero pose in a Tesco aisle with Clubcard price graphics
image.credit: Tesco and BBH London, The Power to Lower Prices (2020) · Little Black Book
